text: According to the Gospel of Mark, Jesus was baptised by John the Baptist in the Jordan River. The event is dated to approximately 28–29 CE during the governorship of Pontius Pilate.

The Pool of Bethesda is described in John 5:2 as having five porticoes. Archaeological excavations in the 19th century identified a double pool structure north of the Temple Mount matching this description.
The Synoptic Gospels — Matthew, Mark, and Luke — narrate the feeding of the five thousand as occurring near Bethsaida. John’s Gospel places the event on the eastern shore of the Sea of Galilee.
The first-century Jewish historian Josephus mentions Jesus twice in his Antiquities of the Jews, completed around 93–94 CE. The longer passage, known as the Testimonium Flavianum, appears in Book 18.
The Roman historian Tacitus references Christ and his execution by Pontius Pilate in his Annals, written around 116 CE. This is the earliest non-Christian reference to Jesus’s death.

The Dead Sea Scrolls, discovered between 1946 and 1956 at Qumran near the Dead Sea, include copies of every book of the Hebrew Bible except Esther. They date from the third century BCE to the first century CE.
The Council of Nicaea was convened by Emperor Constantine in 325 CE in the city of Nicaea in Bithynia. Approximately 300 bishops attended, and the council produced the Nicene Creed.
The Gospel of Thomas was discovered in 1945 near Nag Hammadi in Egypt as part of a cache of Coptic texts. It contains 114 sayings attributed to Jesus, many of which parallel the Synoptic tradition.
Herod the Great ruled Judea from 37 BCE to 4 BCE as a client king under Roman authority. His reign saw extensive building projects including the expansion of the Second Temple in Jerusalem.

The city of Capernaum on the northwestern shore of the Sea of Galilee served as the centre of Jesus’s Galilean ministry according to the Synoptic Gospels. A first-century synagogue and several house structures have been excavated at the site.

The Pauline epistles, traditionally dated between 50 and 67 CE, are the earliest surviving Christian writings. Seven letters — Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Philippians, 1 Thessalonians, and Philemon — are almost universally accepted as authentic.

The Codex Sinaiticus, dating from the fourth century CE, is one of the oldest complete manuscripts of the Christian Bible. It was discovered at Saint Catherine’s Monastery on Mount Sinai in the 19th century.

The siege of Jerusalem in 70 CE resulted in the destruction of the Second Temple by Roman forces under Titus. The event is recorded by Josephus in his Jewish War and had profound consequences for both Judaism and early Christianity.

Pontius Pilate served as the Roman prefect of Judea from 26 to 36 CE. His name appears in the “Pilate Stone,” a limestone block discovered at Caesarea Maritima in 1961, confirming his historical existence outside biblical texts.
The Olivet Discourse is recorded in Matthew 24–25, Mark 13, and Luke 21. Jesus delivers the discourse on the Mount of Olives during the final week before his crucifixion.

The Didache, also known as the Teaching of the Twelve Apostles, is an early Christian text dated to the late first or early second century CE. It provides instructions on baptism, fasting, prayer, and the Eucharist.

The Second Temple period spanned from 516 BCE, when the rebuilt temple was dedicated, to its destruction in 70 CE. This era saw major developments in Jewish sectarianism including the Pharisees, Sadducees, and Essenes.
The Sea of Galilee, also known as Lake Gennesaret or Lake Tiberias, is a freshwater lake in northern Israel. It lies approximately 209 metres below sea level and is fed primarily by the Jordan River.

The twelve apostles, according to the Synoptic Gospels, were Simon Peter, Andrew, James, John, Philip, Bartholomew, Matthew, Thomas, James son of Alphaeus, Thaddaeus, Simon the Zealot, and Judas Iscariot.
The earliest known fragment of the New Testament is the Rylands Library Papyrus P52, a small piece of the Gospel of John dated to the first half of the second century CE.

Matthew 5:3–12 records the Beatitudes, a series of eight blessings spoken by Jesus at the opening of the Sermon on the Mount. Each blessing begins with the formula “Blessed are” and addresses a distinct group: the poor in spirit, those who mourn, the meek, those who hunger for righteousness, the merciful, the pure in heart, the peacemakers, and those persecuted for righteousness.

The Parable of the Good Samaritan appears only in Luke 10:25–37. It describes a man travelling from Jerusalem to Jericho who is stripped, beaten, and left half-dead by robbers. A priest and a Levite pass by on the other side; a Samaritan tends his wounds and arranges for his care at an inn.

The Gospel of John records seven signs performed by Jesus: the turning of water into wine at Cana (2:1–11), the healing of the royal official’s son (4:46–54), the healing at the Pool of Bethesda (5:1–15), the feeding of the five thousand (6:1–14), walking on the sea (6:16–21), the healing of the man born blind (9:1–7), and the raising of Lazarus (11:1–44).

Josephus, in Antiquities 20.9.1, states that Ananus the high priest convened the Sanhedrin and brought before them “the brother of Jesus who was called the Christ, whose name was James, and some others.” He reports that James was stoned to death in 62 CE.

Pliny the Younger, governor of Bithynia and Pontus, wrote a letter to Emperor Trajan around 112 CE describing Christians in his province. He reports that they met before dawn on a fixed day, sang hymns to Christ “as to a god,” and bound themselves by an oath to abstain from theft and adultery.

Ignatius of Antioch wrote seven letters to Christian communities while travelling under guard from Antioch to Rome for his martyrdom around 107 CE. The letters are addressed to the churches at Ephesus, Magnesia, Tralles, Rome, Philadelphia, and Smyrna, and to Polycarp of Smyrna.

Codex Vaticanus, catalogued as B or 03, dates from the fourth century CE and contains most of the Greek Old Testament and the New Testament. The manuscript is housed in the Vatican Library and lacks the Pastoral Epistles, Philemon, and Revelation.

Matthew’s version of the Lord’s Prayer (Matthew 6:9–13) contains seven petitions: the hallowing of God’s name, the coming of the kingdom, the doing of God’s will, daily bread, forgiveness of debts, deliverance from temptation, and deliverance from evil. Luke’s version (Luke 11:2–4) includes the first three and the petitions for bread and forgiveness, omitting the final two.

The Pool of Siloam in Jerusalem was uncovered in 2004 during repair work on a sewer line. Excavators exposed a trapezoidal pool with three sets of five stone steps on three sides, dating to the late Second Temple period. The pool is mentioned in John 9:7 as the place where Jesus sent the man born blind to wash.
Mark 15:21 identifies Simon of Cyrene as “the father of Alexander and Rufus.” Neither Matthew (27:32) nor Luke (23:26) names Alexander and Rufus in their accounts of Simon carrying the cross.

The Mishnah, the earliest written compilation of Jewish oral law, was redacted by Judah ha-Nasi around 200 CE. It is divided into six orders (sedarim) covering agriculture, festivals, women, damages, holy things, and purities, and preserves legal traditions contemporary with the New Testament period.

The Marcionite canon, proposed by Marcion of Sinope around 140 CE, consisted of the Evangelikon, a shortened version of the Gospel of Luke, and the Apostolikon, a collection of ten Pauline epistles. Marcion excluded the entire Old Testament from his canon.

Sepphoris, located approximately six kilometres north-northwest of Nazareth, was the administrative capital of Galilee during the early first century CE. Excavations have revealed a Roman theatre seating approximately four thousand, a market, mosaic-floored villas, and a network of streets laid out on a grid plan.

Papyrus 66 (P66), dated to around 200 CE, preserves a substantial portion of the Gospel of John, including chapters 1 through 21 with some lacunae. It is one of the earliest witnesses to the text of John and forms part of the Bodmer Papyri collection.

Eusebius of Caesarea completed his Ecclesiastical History around 324 CE. The work traces the history of the Christian church from the apostles through the early fourth century, preserving quotations from earlier sources, episcopal succession lists, and accounts of persecutions.

The Parable of the Prodigal Son, recorded only in Luke 15:11–32, describes a younger son who demands his share of the inheritance, departs to a distant country, and squanders his property. After a famine reduces him to feeding pigs, he returns to his father, who runs to meet him and orders a celebration.

Matthew 28:1–10 reports that Mary Magdalene and “the other Mary” visited the tomb at dawn on the first day of the week and encountered an angel who rolled back the stone. Mark 16:1–8 names three women at the tomb: Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome.

Suetonius, in his Life of Claudius (25.4), writes that the emperor “expelled the Jews from Rome because they were continually making disturbances at the instigation of Chrestus.” The passage appears in his Lives of the Twelve Caesars, completed around 121 CE.

The fortress of Masada, situated atop an isolated rock plateau overlooking the Dead Sea, was the site of the final stand of Jewish rebels during the First Jewish–Roman War. Josephus records that the siege ended in 73 or 74 CE when the defenders, led by Eleazar ben Ya’ir, chose mass suicide over capture.

Papyrus 75 (P75), dated to the late second or early third century CE, contains portions of the Gospels of Luke (chapters 3–24) and John (chapters 1–15). The manuscript is notable for its high degree of textual agreement with Codex Vaticanus and is housed in the Vatican Library.

The Epistle to Diognetus, an anonymous Greek apology dating from the late second century CE, describes Christians as living in their own countries but as aliens, sharing all things as citizens and enduring all things as foreigners. The author writes that “what the soul is in the body, that Christians are in the world.”

Mark 10:46–52 records the healing of Bartimaeus, son of Timaeus, a blind beggar sitting beside the road in Jericho. Bartimaeus addresses Jesus as “Son of David” and, after being called, throws off his cloak and comes to Jesus, who restores his sight.

Acts 18:11–12 states that the Apostle Paul remained in Corinth for eighteen months during his second missionary journey. The passage mentions Gallio, proconsul of Achaia, whose tenure is independently confirmed by an inscription discovered at Delphi, allowing scholars to date Paul’s Corinthian stay to approximately 50–51 CE.

Luke 2:1–2 dates the birth of Jesus to the time of a census ordered by Quirinius, governor of Syria. The census of Quirinius is dated by Josephus to around 6 CE. Matthew’s infancy narrative places the birth during the reign of Herod the Great, who died in 4 BCE.

The Epistle of James is addressed to “the twelve tribes in the Dispersion” and is classified as one of the seven Catholic Epistles. The letter opens with an exhortation to count trials as joy, contains extended teaching on faith and works (2:14–26), and closes with instructions on prayer and anointing the sick (5:13–16).

Tertullian of Carthage, writing around 197 CE, composed the Apologeticum, a defence of Christianity addressed to Roman magistrates. He is credited with the earliest surviving use of the Latin term trinitas to describe the relationship of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

Flavius Josephus was born Yosef ben Matityahu in 37 CE to a priestly family in Jerusalem. During the First Jewish–Roman War he commanded Jewish forces in Galilee, surrendered to the Romans at Jotapata in 67 CE, and later received Roman citizenship and a pension from the Flavian emperors.

Mark 4:35–41 recounts Jesus calming a storm on the Sea of Galilee. The passage describes Jesus asleep on a cushion in the stern of the boat when a violent windstorm arises, and the disciples wake him saying, “Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing?”

Codex Bezae (D 05), also known as Codex Cantabrigiensis, dates from the fifth century CE and contains the Gospels and Acts in Greek and Latin on facing pages. It is notable for its distinctive textual variations, including a longer version of the council’s decision in Acts 15 and an inserted pericope about a man working on the Sabbath in Luke 6.

The Essenes are described by Josephus, Philo of Alexandria, and Pliny the Elder as a Jewish sect that practised communal ownership, celibacy, and ritual purity. Pliny locates an Essene settlement on the western shore of the Dead Sea above En Gedi, a location many scholars associate with the site of Qumran.

The term “gospel” derives from the Old English gōdspel, a translation of the Latin bona annuntiatio, which in turn renders the Greek euangelion, meaning “good news.” The four canonical Gospels were composed in Koine Greek between approximately 65 and 100 CE.

Matthew 17:24–27 records the temple tax pericope, found only in Matthew’s Gospel. Jesus instructs Peter to cast a hook into the Sea of Galilee: “Take the first fish that comes up, and when you open its mouth you will find a shekel. Take that and give it to them for me and for yourself.”

Irenaeus of Lyon, writing around 180 CE, composed Against Heresies, a five-book refutation of Gnostic teachings. In Book 3, he names the four canonical Gospels and argues that their number — four — is fitting because there are four zones of the world and four principal winds.

Herod Antipas, a son of Herod the Great, ruled as tetrarch of Galilee and Perea from 4 BCE until his exile in 39 CE. The Gospels name him as responsible for the imprisonment and execution of John the Baptist (Mark 6:14–29) and as the ruler before whom Jesus appeared during his trial (Luke 23:6–12).

Luke 23:26 describes Simon of Cyrene, “coming in from the country,” as the man seized by Roman soldiers and compelled to carry the cross behind Jesus on the way to Golgotha. The passage uses the Greek verb opisthen (“behind”) to describe his position relative to Jesus.

The Epistle of Barnabas, a Greek theological treatise dated to the late first or early second century CE, interprets the Old Testament allegorically, arguing that the Mosaic covenant was never intended to be observed literally by the Jewish people. The text was included alongside the New Testament in Codex Sinaiticus.

Tacitus, in Annals 15.44, records that Nero, to suppress the rumour that he had started the Great Fire of Rome in 64 CE, “fastened the guilt” on a group he calls Christians. Tacitus describes the punishments inflicted on them, including being covered with animal skins and torn by dogs, and being crucified and burned as torches.

Matthew 13:3–9 presents the Parable of the Sower: a sower scatters seed that falls on four types of ground — the path (eaten by birds), rocky soil (scorched by the sun), among thorns (choked), and good soil (producing grain a hundredfold, sixtyfold, and thirtyfold).

John 4:5–29 records Jesus’s encounter with a Samaritan woman at Jacob’s well near the town of Sychar. The passage notes that the well was located on ground Jacob had given to his son Joseph and that Jesus, tired from the journey, sat by the well around the sixth hour.

Papias, bishop of Hierapolis in Phrygia, wrote a five-volume work titled Expositions of the Sayings of the Lord in the early second century CE. The text survives only in fragments preserved by Eusebius and Irenaeus. Eusebius quotes Papias as stating that Mark, “having become Peter’s interpreter, wrote down accurately everything that he remembered of the Lord’s words and deeds.”

Matthew 25:31–46 records the judgement of the nations, commonly called the Parable of the Sheep and Goats. The Son of Man, seated on his throne, separates people “as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats,” inviting those on his right into the kingdom and sending those on his left into eternal punishment.

Clement of Rome composed a letter to the Corinthian church around 96 CE, known as 1 Clement. The letter addresses a dispute in which younger members had deposed the established leadership, and it is among the earliest surviving Christian documents outside the New Testament.

The Aramaic expression bar nasha, rendered in Greek as ho huios tou anthrōpou (“the Son of Man”), appears over eighty times in the four Gospels. In all four canonical accounts, it is the title Jesus most frequently uses to refer to himself.

1 Corinthians 15:3–8 preserves an early creedal formula widely regarded as pre-Pauline. The passage states that Christ died, was buried, and was raised, and then appeared to Cephas, to the Twelve, to more than five hundred brothers and sisters at one time, to James, to all the apostles, and lastly to Paul.

Matthew 22:15–22, Mark 12:13–17, and Luke 20:20–26 record the question about paying the census tax to Caesar. Jesus asks to see the coin used for the tax and, upon inspecting the denarius bearing the emperor’s image and inscription, replies, “Give back to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s.”

Luke 24:50–53 places the Ascension at Bethany on the same day as the resurrection. Acts 1:9–12 locates the event at the Mount of Olives, forty days after the resurrection, and specifies that Jesus was “lifted up” before being hidden by a cloud.

Lucian of Samosata, a Greek satirist writing around 165 CE, refers to Jesus in his work The Death of Peregrinus. He describes Christians as worshipping “the man who was crucified in Palestine,” whom he identifies as the founder of their cult.

John 11:1–44 records the raising of Lazarus of Bethany, the brother of Mary and Martha. The passage specifies that Jesus arrived in Bethany four days after Lazarus had been buried and that the tomb was a cave with a stone laid across the entrance.

The Epistle of Polycarp to the Philippians, dated to the early second century CE, is one of the earliest surviving Christian writings outside the New Testament. Polycarp quotes from or alludes to 1 Peter, 1 John, and multiple Pauline letters, providing early evidence for the circulation of these texts.

The longer ending of Mark (Mark 16:9–20) is absent from the two oldest complete Greek manuscripts, Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, both dated to the fourth century CE. The ending is present in Codex Bezae and the majority of later Greek manuscripts.

The Syriac Sinaiticus, dated to the late fourth or early fifth century CE, is one of the oldest surviving manuscripts of the Gospels in Syriac. It preserves the Old Syriac version, distinct from the later standard Peshitta translation, and was discovered at Saint Catherine’s Monastery on Mount Sinai.
Mark 6:3 identifies Jesus as a carpenter (Greek tektōn) and names his brothers as James, Joses, Judas, and Simon. The verse also refers to his sisters, though they are not named.

The philosopher Celsus wrote The True Word (Alēthēs Logos) around 175 CE, the first comprehensive pagan critique of Christianity. The text survives only in quotations embedded in Origen’s refutation, Against Celsus, composed approximately seventy years later.

Mark 8:1–10 and Matthew 15:32–39 record the feeding of the four thousand in the region of the Decapolis. The accounts state that seven loaves of bread and a few small fish fed a crowd of four thousand men, besides women and children, and that seven baskets of broken pieces were collected afterwards.

The Muratorian Fragment, a seventh- or eighth-century Latin manuscript preserving a second-century original, contains the earliest known list of books accepted as authoritative in the Roman church. The fragment lists the four Gospels, Acts, thirteen epistles of Paul, Jude, two epistles of John, the Wisdom of Solomon, and the Revelation of John and of Peter.

John 19:26–27 records that, during the crucifixion, Jesus saw his mother and the beloved disciple standing near the cross. He said to his mother, “Woman, here is your son,” and to the disciple, “Here is your mother.” The passage concludes that “from that hour the disciple took her into his own home.”

Justin Martyr, writing around 155 CE, addressed his First Apology to the Emperor Antoninus Pius, the Emperor Marcus Aurelius, the Senate, and the whole Roman people. He describes the weekly worship of Christians, noting that “the memoirs of the apostles” — a term he uses interchangeably with “Gospels” — are read aloud in the assembly.

Luke 1:46–55 records the Magnificat, Mary’s hymn of praise spoken during her visit to Elizabeth. The hymn opens, “My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit rejoices in God my Saviour,” and draws extensively on language from the Song of Hannah in 1 Samuel 2:1–10.

Mara bar Serapion, a Syriac philosopher, wrote a letter to his son that includes a reference to a “wise king” of the Jews who was executed. The letter asks, “What advantage did the Jews gain from executing their wise king?” The text is preserved in a sixth- or seventh-century Syriac manuscript housed in the British Library.

The Sermon on the Mount, recorded in Matthew 5–7, is the first of five major discourses in Matthew’s Gospel. It begins with the Beatitudes, includes the antitheses on the law (5:21–48), instruction on almsgiving, prayer, and fasting (6:1–18), and the Lord’s Prayer (6:9–13), and concludes with the parable of the wise and foolish builders (7:24–27).
